Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let
$A=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}A^j$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded $k$-vector space; its tensor
maps use the convention in [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]]. An
**uncurved cohomological A∞-algebra in the unsuspended convention** is a
sequence of homogeneous $k$-linear maps

$$m_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow A,\qquad |m_n|=2-n, \qquad n\ge1,$$

such that for every $n\ge1$ the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to A$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st} m_{r+1+t}\bigl(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t}\bigr)=0.$$

Here $1$ denotes the identity map of $A$, the tensor maps use the Koszul rule,
and the displayed sign $(-1)^{r+st}$ is part of the fixed convention. The
degree condition means that for homogeneous inputs of degrees $j_1,\ldots,j_n$,
$m_n$ has output degree $j_1+\cdots+j_n+2-n$.

“Uncurved” means no arity-zero operation $m_0$ is included. “Nonunital” means
that no unit is part of this definition. A unit or a strict-unit condition on
higher operations is additional data and must be stated separately. No graded
commutativity is assumed for $m_2$.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]), and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be graded
$k$-vector spaces. A $k$-vector space is a unital left $k$-module as in
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. Tensor powers are formed using the tensor
products of
[[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]. If $f_i:V_i\to W_i$ are homogeneous
linear maps of degrees $d_i$, and $x_i\in V_i$ are homogeneous of degrees
$p_i$, the graded tensor map is defined on pure tensors by

$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{i>j}d_i p_j} f_1(x_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n(x_n).$$

It is extended linearly. In particular, for two maps,
$(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{|g||x|}f(x)\otimes g(y)$.

For homogeneous $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$, the
**Koszul sign** of reordering them to
$x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}$ is

$$\epsilon(\sigma;x_1,\ldots,x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{\substack{i<j\\\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)}} |x_{\sigma(i)}||x_{\sigma(j)}|}.$$

Thus swapping two adjacent homogeneous factors $x,y$ contributes
$(-1)^{|x||y|}$. Every tensor of maps, permutation, unshuffle, and symmetric
power below uses this same convention. A sign is a scalar in $k$ determined
only by the parity of the displayed integer exponent.

derivations.claim: For $n=1$, the only triple $(r,s,t)$ is $(0,1,0)$, so [F1] is exactly $m_1m_1=0$.

For $n=2$, the triples are $(0,1,1)$, $(1,1,0)$, and $(0,2,0)$; their coefficients are $-1,-1,+1$. Hence [F1] gives $m_1m_2-m_2(m_1\otimes1)-m_2(1\otimes m_1)=0$. On homogeneous $a,b$, [F2] makes the last term $(-1)^{|a|}m_2(a,m_1b)$, which is the signed derivation rule.

For $n=3$, the triples with $s=1$ contribute the three terms $m_3(m_1\otimes1\otimes1)$, $m_3(1\otimes m_1\otimes1)$, $m_3(1\otimes1\otimes m_1)$, each with sign $+1$; $s=2$ contributes $m_2(m_2\otimes1)-m_2(1\otimes m_2)$; and $s=3$ contributes $m_1m_3$. Their sum is the third displayed identity.

sequence of homogeneous $k$-linear maps

$$m_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow A,\qquad |m_n|=2-n, \qquad n\ge1,$$

such that for every $n\ge1$ the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to A$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st} m_{r+1+t}\bigl(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t}\bigr)=0.$$

Here $1$ denotes the identity map of $A$, the tensor maps use the Koszul rule,
and the displayed sign $(-1)^{r+st}$ is part of the fixed convention. The

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit. A **cohomological differential graded
algebra over $R$** (cohomological DGA) consists of a $\mathbb Z$-graded
$R$-module $A=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}A^n$, an $R$-bilinear associative
multiplication $A^p\times A^q\to A^{p+q}$ with a unit $1\in A^0$ and central
$R$-action, and $R$-linear maps $d^n:A^n\to A^{n+1}$ such that
$d^{n+1}d^n=0$. The degree convention and square-zero differential are those
of a cochain complex ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]); the
ungraded multiplication and unit satisfy the $R$-algebra convention in
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]].

For homogeneous $a\in A^p$ and $b\in A^q$, require the signed Leibniz rule
$$d^{p+q}(ab)=d^p(a)b+(-1)^p a d^q(b).$$
No symmetry condition $ab=(-1)^{pq}ba$ is imposed on homogeneous elements of
degrees $p$ and $q$. In particular, this definition fixes the cohomological
sign convention and does not assert any formality, derived-category, or
Hochschild-cohomology result.

The unit is automatically closed: applying the Leibniz rule to $1\cdot1$
gives $d(1)=d(1)+d(1)$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $d(1)=0$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.

Let $(A,m_n)$ be an uncurved cohomological A∞-algebra with the unsuspended
convention of [[def-a-infinity-algebra]]. Its first three identities are

$$m_1m_1=0,$$

$$m_1m_2=m_2(m_1\otimes1+1\otimes m_1),$$

and

$$m_1m_3+m_3(m_1\otimes1\otimes1+1\otimes m_1\otimes1+1\otimes1\otimes m_1) +m_2(m_2\otimes1)-m_2(1\otimes m_2)=0.$$

In particular, $m_1$ is a cochain differential and a signed derivation of
$m_2$. The third identity explicitly gives the associator
$m_2(m_2\otimes1)-m_2(1\otimes m_2)$ as the negative of the displayed
$m_1,m_3$ terms.

derivations.claim: The maps have the required degrees: $m_1=d$ has degree $+1=2-1$, $m_2=\mu$ has degree $0=2-2$, and each zero map $m_n$ for $n\ge3$ is a homogeneous map of degree $2-n$. The ring and field hypotheses agree by [F3].
By [F2], $d^2=0$ and $d$ satisfies the signed Leibniz rule, so the first two identities of [F4] hold for $m_1=d$ and $m_2=\mu$.
Since $m_3=0$, the third identity of [F4] reduces to $\mu(\mu\otimes1)-\mu(1\otimes\mu)=0$, which is associativity from [F2].

For $n\ge4$, any nonzero summand in the Stasheff sum would require both the inner arity $s$ and the outer arity $r+1+t$ to lie in $\{1,2\}$. But $n=r+s+t=s+(r+1+t)-1\le3$, contradicting $n\ge4$. Thus every term in each such sum is zero.

expression is closed, so its cohomology class is defined.

Let $k$ be a characteristic-zero field ([[def-field]]), meaning
$\operatorname{char}(k)=0$ under [[def-ring-characteristic]]. By
[[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]], $k$ is a commutative ring. Let
$W=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}W^j$ be a graded $k$-vector space. For $n\ge1$,
define the graded symmetric power

$$S^n(W)=W^{\otimes_k n}/J_n,$$

where $J_n$ is spanned by the differences obtained by replacing any adjacent
homogeneous factors $x\otimes y$ by
$(-1)^{|x||y|}y\otimes x$ inside a pure tensor. Write
$w_1\odot\cdots\odot w_n$ for the image of a tensor and set

$$S^c(W)=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}S^n(W).$$

The **reduced shuffle coproduct** is the degree-zero linear map
$\bar\Delta:S^c(W)\to S^c(W)\otimes_k S^c(W)$ given on a homogeneous pure
symmetric tensor by

$$\bar\Delta(w_1\odot\cdots\odot w_n) =\sum_{p=1}^{n-1}\ \sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sh}(p,n-p)} \epsilon(\sigma;w_1,\ldots,w_n) (w_{\sigma(1)}\odot\cdots\odot w_{\sigma(p)})\otimes (w_{\sigma(p+1)}\odot\cdots\odot w_{\sigma(n)}),$$

where
$\operatorname{Sh}(p,n-p)=\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(1)<\cdots<\sigma(p),\
\sigma(p+1)<\cdots<\sigma(n)\}$, and $\epsilon$ is the Koszul sign of
[[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]].
For $n=1$ the sum is empty and $\bar\Delta(w)=0$. This is a reduced, hence
noncounital coalgebra convention; no arity-zero summand is included. The next
lemmas verify its coproduct laws, conilpotence, and cofree universal property.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]), and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be graded
$k$-vector spaces. A $k$-vector space is a unital left $k$-module as in
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. Tensor powers are formed using the tensor
products of
[[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]. If $f_i:V_i\to W_i$ are homogeneous
linear maps of degrees $d_i$, and $x_i\in V_i$ are homogeneous of degrees
$p_i$, the graded tensor map is defined on pure tensors by

$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{i>j}d_i p_j} f_1(x_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n(x_n).$$

It is extended linearly. In particular, for two maps,
$(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{|g||x|}f(x)\otimes g(y)$.

For homogeneous $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$, the
**Koszul sign** of reordering them to
$x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}$ is

$$\epsilon(\sigma;x_1,\ldots,x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{\substack{i<j\\\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)}} |x_{\sigma(i)}||x_{\sigma(j)}|}.$$

Thus swapping two adjacent homogeneous factors $x,y$ contributes
$(-1)^{|x||y|}$. Every tensor of maps, permutation, unshuffle, and symmetric
power below uses this same convention. A sign is a scalar in $k$ determined
only by the parity of the displayed integer exponent.

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with identity $1_R$ and zero $0_R$. For
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $n \cdot 1_R$ be the additive natural power of $1_R$ in
the abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$ ([[def-group-power]], [[def-group]]): thus
$0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ and $\sigma(n)\cdot 1_R = n \cdot 1_R + 1_R$. Put

$$T_R \;:=\; \{\, n \in \mathbb{N} \;:\; n \ge 1 \text{ and } n \cdot 1_R = 0_R \,\} \;\subseteq\; \mathbb{N}.$$

The **characteristic** of $R$ is

$$\operatorname{char}(R) \;:=\; \begin{cases} \min T_R & \text{if } T_R \ne \varnothing, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } T_R = \varnothing.\end{cases}$$

**Why the least element exists.** $T_R$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$, so when it
is nonempty it has a least element by the well-ordering principle
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), and that element is unique: two least members
are below one another and hence equal by antisymmetry of the natural-number
order ([[thm-nat-linear-order]], [[def-nat-order]]). So
$\operatorname{char}(R)$ is a well-defined natural number in both cases.

**The clause $n \ge 1$ is not decoration.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and $0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ holds in every ring, so
without that clause $T_R$ would always contain $0$ and the definition would say
nothing.

**Convention: the value in the empty case is $0$, and this is the OPPOSITE of
the convention for the order of a group element.** [[def-order-in-a-group]]
writes $\operatorname{ord}(g) = \infty$ when no positive power of $g$ is the
identity. Here the value in the corresponding case is the natural number $0$,
not a symbol $\infty$. A reader coming straight from
[[def-order-in-a-group]] should notice the difference: it is deliberate, it is
the standard convention for the characteristic, and it is what makes the
divisibility statement of [[lem-characteristic-and-additive-order]] uniform
across the two cases.

**$\operatorname{char}(R)$ is a natural number, hence a set, not an element of
$R$.** A natural number in this library is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so $\operatorname{char}(R) \notin R$ in general and
the expression $n \cdot 1_R$ is not a product in $R$ but the additive multiple
just described.

**Dictionary for fields.** When $R$ is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]), the element
$n \cdot 1_F$ is exactly the canonical natural $\iota(n)$ of
[[def-canonical-natural]]; this is proved, not assumed, in
[[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]. So for a field
$T_F = \{\, n \ge 1 : \iota(n) = 0_F \,\}$ and the characteristic is the least
$n \ge 1$ with $\iota(n) = 0_F$, or $0$ if there is none.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.

derivations.claim: The quotient relations are generated by adjacent graded swaps. In each unshuffle summand of [F1], swapping adjacent inputs either changes their order inside one output block, where the same quotient relation applies, or moves them between blocks, where the graded flip in the target tensor product contributes exactly $(-1)^{|x||y|}$. The unshuffle terms are reindexed by this swap, so [F1] and [F2] give the same output class; hence $\bar\Delta$ descends to $S^n(W)$.

Both iterated coproducts $(\bar\Delta\otimes1)\bar\Delta$ and $(1\otimes\bar\Delta)\bar\Delta$ on a length-$n$ tensor sum over the same ordered decompositions of its labels into three nonempty, internally ordered blocks. In either parenthesization the sign is the Koszul sign of the single permutation that places those labels into the same three blocks. The terms therefore agree one by one, proving coassociativity.

The graded flip interchanging the two tensor factors sends a $(p,n-p)$-unshuffle to the complementary $(n-p,p)$-unshuffle. Its block-swap sign is exactly the Koszul sign for moving every factor in the first block past every factor in the second. Thus the terms pair with identical coefficients after the graded flip, proving graded cocommutativity.

$\operatorname{char}(k)=0$ under [[def-ring-characteristic]]. By
[[lem-field-is-a-commutative-ring]], $k$ is a commutative ring. Let
$W=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}W^j$ be a graded $k$-vector space. For $n\ge1$,
define the graded symmetric power

$$S^n(W)=W^{\otimes_k n}/J_n,$$

where $J_n$ is spanned by the differences obtained by replacing any adjacent
homogeneous factors $x\otimes y$ by
$(-1)^{|x||y|}y\otimes x$ inside a pure tensor. Write
$w_1\odot\cdots\odot w_n$ for the image of a tensor and set

$$S^c(W)=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}S^n(W).$$

The **reduced shuffle coproduct** is the degree-zero linear map
$\bar\Delta:S^c(W)\to S^c(W)\otimes_k S^c(W)$ given on a homogeneous pure
symmetric tensor by

$$\bar\Delta(w_1\odot\cdots\odot w_n) =\sum_{p=1}^{n-1}\ \sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Sh}(p,n-p)} \epsilon(\sigma;w_1,\ldots,w_n) (w_{\sigma(1)}\odot\cdots\odot w_{\sigma(p)})\otimes (w_{\sigma(p+1)}\odot\cdots\odot w_{\sigma(n)}),$$

where
$\operatorname{Sh}(p,n-p)=\{\sigma\in S_n:\sigma(1)<\cdots<\sigma(p),\
\sigma(p+1)<\cdots<\sigma(n)\}$, and $\epsilon$ is the Koszul sign of
[[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]].
For $n=1$ the sum is empty and $\bar\Delta(w)=0$. This is a reduced, hence
noncounital coalgebra convention; no arity-zero summand is included. The next
lemmas verify its coproduct laws, conilpotence, and cofree universal property.

Let $S^c(W)$ and $\bar\Delta$ be as in
[[def-reduced-graded-symmetric-coalgebra]]. The reduced coproduct is
well-defined on the graded-symmetric quotient, is coassociative and
graded-cocommutative, and is conilpotent: every element is killed by a
sufficiently long iterated reduced coproduct. Its primitive subspace
($\ker\bar\Delta$) is exactly $S^1(W)=W$.

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with identity $1_R$ and zero $0_R$. For
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $n \cdot 1_R$ be the additive natural power of $1_R$ in
the abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$ ([[def-group-power]], [[def-group]]): thus
$0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ and $\sigma(n)\cdot 1_R = n \cdot 1_R + 1_R$. Put

$$T_R \;:=\; \{\, n \in \mathbb{N} \;:\; n \ge 1 \text{ and } n \cdot 1_R = 0_R \,\} \;\subseteq\; \mathbb{N}.$$

The **characteristic** of $R$ is

$$\operatorname{char}(R) \;:=\; \begin{cases} \min T_R & \text{if } T_R \ne \varnothing, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } T_R = \varnothing.\end{cases}$$

**Why the least element exists.** $T_R$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$, so when it
is nonempty it has a least element by the well-ordering principle
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), and that element is unique: two least members
are below one another and hence equal by antisymmetry of the natural-number
order ([[thm-nat-linear-order]], [[def-nat-order]]). So
$\operatorname{char}(R)$ is a well-defined natural number in both cases.

**The clause $n \ge 1$ is not decoration.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and $0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ holds in every ring, so
without that clause $T_R$ would always contain $0$ and the definition would say
nothing.

**Convention: the value in the empty case is $0$, and this is the OPPOSITE of
the convention for the order of a group element.** [[def-order-in-a-group]]
writes $\operatorname{ord}(g) = \infty$ when no positive power of $g$ is the
identity. Here the value in the corresponding case is the natural number $0$,
not a symbol $\infty$. A reader coming straight from
[[def-order-in-a-group]] should notice the difference: it is deliberate, it is
the standard convention for the characteristic, and it is what makes the
divisibility statement of [[lem-characteristic-and-additive-order]] uniform
across the two cases.

**$\operatorname{char}(R)$ is a natural number, hence a set, not an element of
$R$.** A natural number in this library is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so $\operatorname{char}(R) \notin R$ in general and
the expression $n \cdot 1_R$ is not a product in $R$ but the additive multiple
just described.

$n \cdot 1_F$ is exactly the canonical natural $\iota(n)$ of
[[def-canonical-natural]]; this is proved, not assumed, in
[[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]. So for a field
$T_F = \{\, n \ge 1 : \iota(n) = 0_F \,\}$ and the characteristic is the least
$n \ge 1$ with $\iota(n) = 0_F$, or $0$ if there is none.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]), and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be graded
$k$-vector spaces. A $k$-vector space is a unital left $k$-module as in
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. Tensor powers are formed using the tensor
products of
[[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]. If $f_i:V_i\to W_i$ are homogeneous
linear maps of degrees $d_i$, and $x_i\in V_i$ are homogeneous of degrees
$p_i$, the graded tensor map is defined on pure tensors by

$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{i>j}d_i p_j} f_1(x_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n(x_n).$$

It is extended linearly. In particular, for two maps,
$(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{|g||x|}f(x)\otimes g(y)$.

For homogeneous $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$, the
**Koszul sign** of reordering them to
$x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}$ is

$$\epsilon(\sigma;x_1,\ldots,x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{\substack{i<j\\\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)}} |x_{\sigma(i)}||x_{\sigma(j)}|}.$$

Thus swapping two adjacent homogeneous factors $x,y$ contributes
$(-1)^{|x||y|}$. Every tensor of maps, permutation, unshuffle, and symmetric
power below uses this same convention. A sign is a scalar in $k$ determined
only by the parity of the displayed integer exponent.

derivations.claim: The square $Q^2$ is a coderivation of degree $2$. Indeed, applying the coderivation equation twice gives $\bar\Delta Q^2 =(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)^2\bar\Delta =(Q^2\otimes1+1\otimes Q^2)\bar\Delta,$ because the two cross terms are $Q\otimes Q$ and $-Q\otimes Q$ by [F4].

On an input of symmetric length $n$, the projection $\pi_1Q^2$ can be nonzero only when the first application of $Q$ consumes $i$ inputs by $q_i$ and the second consumes the resulting $q_i$ output together with all $n-i$ unused inputs by $q_{n-i+1}$. Let $(V,Q)$ be an L∞-algebra in the shifted convention of
[[def-shifted-coalgebra-l-infinity-algebra]], with $W=V[1]$ and corestrictions
$q_n:S^n(W)\to W$. A **complete filtered L∞-algebra** is this data together
with a descending filtration by graded subspaces

$$F^1W\supseteq F^2W\supseteq F^3W\supseteq\cdots$$

such that both of the following conditions hold:

1. The natural map from $W$ to the set of compatible cosets
   $$(w_r+F^rW)_{r\ge1},\qquad w_{r+1}-w_r\in F^rW,$$
   is a bijection. Thus the filtration is separated and complete.
2. For every $n\ge1$ and positive integers $r_1,\ldots,r_n$,
   $$q_n(F^{r_1}W,\ldots,F^{r_n}W) \subseteq F^{r_1+\cdots+r_n}W.$$

This definition imposes an algebraic filtration topology only; it makes no
analytic convergence assertion. The next theorem proves that the
Maurer–Cartan series converges for each $w\in F^1W^0$.

A **field** is a set $F$ equipped with two binary operations $+$ (addition) and
$\cdot$ (multiplication) and two distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$ of $F$,
satisfying:

- **(A)** $(F, +)$ is an abelian group with identity $0$: addition is
  associative and commutative, $x + 0 = x$ for all $x$, and every $x$ has an
  additive inverse $-x$ with $x + (-x) = 0$.
- **(M)** Multiplication is associative and commutative **on all of $F$**, and
  $x \cdot 1 = x$ for every $x \in F$; moreover $(F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot)$ is an
  abelian group with identity $1$, so every $x \ne 0$ has a multiplicative inverse
  $x^{-1}$ with $x \cdot x^{-1} = 1$.
- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

We write $x - y := x + (-y)$ and $x/y := x \cdot y^{-1}$ (for $y \ne 0$), and
abbreviate $x \cdot y$ as $xy$.

Let $R$ be a ring ([[def-ring]]) with identity $1_R$ and zero $0_R$. For
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ let $n \cdot 1_R$ be the additive natural power of $1_R$ in
the abelian group $(R,+,0_R)$ ([[def-group-power]], [[def-group]]): thus
$0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ and $\sigma(n)\cdot 1_R = n \cdot 1_R + 1_R$. Put

$$T_R \;:=\; \{\, n \in \mathbb{N} \;:\; n \ge 1 \text{ and } n \cdot 1_R = 0_R \,\} \;\subseteq\; \mathbb{N}.$$

The **characteristic** of $R$ is

$$\operatorname{char}(R) \;:=\; \begin{cases} \min T_R & \text{if } T_R \ne \varnothing, \\[2pt] 0 & \text{if } T_R = \varnothing.\end{cases}$$

**Why the least element exists.** $T_R$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$, so when it
is nonempty it has a least element by the well-ordering principle
([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]), and that element is unique: two least members
are below one another and hence equal by antisymmetry of the natural-number
order ([[thm-nat-linear-order]], [[def-nat-order]]). So
$\operatorname{char}(R)$ is a well-defined natural number in both cases.

**The clause $n \ge 1$ is not decoration.** $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]) and $0 \cdot 1_R = 0_R$ holds in every ring, so
without that clause $T_R$ would always contain $0$ and the definition would say
nothing.

**Convention: the value in the empty case is $0$, and this is the OPPOSITE of
the convention for the order of a group element.** [[def-order-in-a-group]]
writes $\operatorname{ord}(g) = \infty$ when no positive power of $g$ is the
identity. Here the value in the corresponding case is the natural number $0$,
not a symbol $\infty$. A reader coming straight from
[[def-order-in-a-group]] should notice the difference: it is deliberate, it is
the standard convention for the characteristic, and it is what makes the
divisibility statement of [[lem-characteristic-and-additive-order]] uniform
across the two cases.

**$\operatorname{char}(R)$ is a natural number, hence a set, not an element of
$R$.** A natural number in this library is a von Neumann natural
([[def-natural-numbers]]), so $\operatorname{char}(R) \notin R$ in general and
the expression $n \cdot 1_R$ is not a product in $R$ but the additive multiple
just described.

**Dictionary for fields.** When $R$ is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]), the element
$n \cdot 1_F$ is exactly the canonical natural $\iota(n)$ of
[[def-canonical-natural]]; this is proved, not assumed, in
[[lem-integer-multiples-agree-with-canonical-natural]]. So for a field
$T_F = \{\, n \ge 1 : \iota(n) = 0_F \,\}$ and the characteristic is the least
$n \ge 1$ with $\iota(n) = 0_F$, or $0$ if there is none.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.

derivations.claim: For every $n\ge1$, [F1] with each $r_i=1$ gives $q_n(w,\ldots,w)\in F^nW$. Since $q_n$ has degree $+1$ and $w$ has degree zero, each term lies in $F^nW^1$. By [F2], division by $n!$ is defined and does not change the filtration level.
Fix $r\ge1$. If $n\ge r$, then $F^nW\subseteq F^rW$, so every term of index $n\ge r$ vanishes in $W/F^rW$. Therefore the partial sums stabilize modulo $F^rW$ once the upper index is at least $r-1$.

These stabilized residues are compatible under the quotient maps $W/F^{r+1}W\to W/F^rW$, because they come from the same nested partial sums. Completeness in [F1] gives a unique element of $W$ having all these residues. The partial sums converge to it in the filtration topology.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let
$A=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}A^j$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded $k$-vector space; its tensor
maps use the convention in [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]]. An
**uncurved cohomological A∞-algebra in the unsuspended convention** is a
sequence of homogeneous $k$-linear maps

$$m_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow A,\qquad |m_n|=2-n, \qquad n\ge1,$$

such that for every $n\ge1$ the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to A$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st} m_{r+1+t}\bigl(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t}\bigr)=0.$$

Here $1$ denotes the identity map of $A$, the tensor maps use the Koszul rule,
and the displayed sign $(-1)^{r+st}$ is part of the fixed convention. The
degree condition means that for homogeneous inputs of degrees $j_1,\ldots,j_n$,
$m_n$ has output degree $j_1+\cdots+j_n+2-n$.

“Uncurved” means no arity-zero operation $m_0$ is included. “Nonunital” means
that no unit is part of this definition. A unit or a strict-unit condition on
higher operations is additional data and must be stated separately. No graded
commutativity is assumed for $m_2$.

- **(D)** Multiplication distributes over addition: $x \cdot (y + z) = x\cdot y + x\cdot z$.

derivations.claim: The zero map $m_1$ is homogeneous of degree $+1$, field multiplication $m_2$ has degree zero on $A^0$, and every zero map $m_n$ for $n\ge3$ is homogeneous of degree $2-n$. Thus the degrees match [F1].
For $n=3$, the only possibly nonzero terms are $m_2(m_2\otimes1)-m_2(1\otimes m_2)$. They agree by associativity in [F2], so their difference is zero.

For $n=1$ every Stasheff summand contains $m_1$, so the sum is zero. For $n=2$, the only potentially nonzero outer operation is $m_1m_2$, but $m_1=0$; all summands containing an inner $m_1$ also vanish.
For $n\ge4$, a nonzero summand would require both inner and outer operations to have arity two, which forces $n=s+(r+1+t)-1\le3$. Therefore all terms vanish in these arities as well.
The defining identity holds in every arity by steps 2.1, 1.2 and 2.2, so the stated operations form an A∞-algebra.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit. A **cohomological differential graded
algebra over $R$** (cohomological DGA) consists of a $\mathbb Z$-graded
$R$-module $A=\bigoplus_{n\in\mathbb Z}A^n$, an $R$-bilinear associative
multiplication $A^p\times A^q\to A^{p+q}$ with a unit $1\in A^0$ and central
$R$-action, and $R$-linear maps $d^n:A^n\to A^{n+1}$ such that
$d^{n+1}d^n=0$. The degree convention and square-zero differential are those
of a cochain complex ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]); the
ungraded multiplication and unit satisfy the $R$-algebra convention in
[[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]].

For homogeneous $a\in A^p$ and $b\in A^q$, require the signed Leibniz rule
$$d^{p+q}(ab)=d^p(a)b+(-1)^p a d^q(b).$$
No symmetry condition $ab=(-1)^{pq}ba$ is imposed on homogeneous elements of
degrees $p$ and $q$. In particular, this definition fixes the cohomological
sign convention and does not assert any formality, derived-category, or
Hochschild-cohomology result.

The unit is automatically closed: applying the Leibniz rule to $1\cdot1$
gives $d(1)=d(1)+d(1)$, so cancellation in the additive group gives $d(1)=0$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]), with addition $+$, multiplication $\cdot$,
and distinguished elements $0 \ne 1$. Then

1. $(F, +, \cdot, 0, 1)$ is a ring ([[def-ring]]), and it is commutative
   ([[def-commutative-ring]]), with $1 \ne 0$;
2. $F$ is an integral domain ([[def-zero-divisor-and-integral-domain]]);
3. $F$ is a division ring ([[def-division-ring]]), and hence a commutative
   division ring.

The field structure is not changed by this: the ring operations are the field
operations, and the ring's zero and identity are the field's $0$ and $1$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $(A,d,\mu)$ be a cohomological differential graded
algebra over $k$ in the convention of
[[def-differential-graded-algebra]]. Put $m_1=d$, $m_2=\mu$, and $m_n=0$ for
all $n\ge3$. Then these maps make $A$ an uncurved cohomological A∞-algebra
in the unsuspended convention of [[def-a-infinity-algebra]].

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let
$A=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}A^j$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded $k$-vector space; its tensor
maps use the convention in [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]]. An
**uncurved cohomological A∞-algebra in the unsuspended convention** is a
sequence of homogeneous $k$-linear maps

$$m_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow A,\qquad |m_n|=2-n, \qquad n\ge1,$$

such that for every $n\ge1$ the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to A$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st} m_{r+1+t}\bigl(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t}\bigr)=0.$$

Here $1$ denotes the identity map of $A$, the tensor maps use the Koszul rule,
and the displayed sign $(-1)^{r+st}$ is part of the fixed convention. The
degree condition means that for homogeneous inputs of degrees $j_1,\ldots,j_n$,
$m_n$ has output degree $j_1+\cdots+j_n+2-n$.

“Uncurved” means no arity-zero operation $m_0$ is included. “Nonunital” means
that no unit is part of this definition. A unit or a strict-unit condition on
higher operations is additional data and must be stated separately. No graded
commutativity is assumed for $m_2$.

Let $A$ and $B$ be uncurved cohomological A∞-algebras in the convention of
[[def-a-infinity-algebra]]. An **A∞-morphism** $f:A\to B$ is a family of
homogeneous maps

$$f_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow B,\qquad |f_n|=1-n,\qquad n\ge1,$$

such that, for every $n\ge1$, the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to B$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,s,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st}f_{r+1+t}(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s^A\otimes1^{\otimes t}) =\sum_{q=1}^{n}\ \sum_{\substack{i_1+\cdots+i_q=n\\i_j\ge1}} (-1)^{\eta(i_1,\ldots,i_q)} m_q^B(f_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{i_q}),$$

where
$\eta(i_1,\ldots,i_q)=\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}(q-j)(i_j-1)$ and all tensor maps
use [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]]. The identity at $n=1$ says
that $f_1$ is a cochain map from $(A,m_1^A)$ to $(B,m_1^B)$.

An A∞-morphism is an **A∞ quasi-isomorphism** if $f_1$ induces an isomorphism
on cohomology, where
$H^j(A,m_1^A)=\ker(m_1^A:A^j\to A^{j+1})/\operatorname{im}(m_1^A:A^{j-1}\to A^j)$
and likewise for $B$. This definition imposes no unit condition on $f$.

Let $A$ be an uncurved A∞-algebra ([[def-a-infinity-algebra]]). A
**minimal A∞-model** for $A$ is an
uncurved A∞-algebra $H$ with $m_1^H=0$, together with an A∞
quasi-isomorphism $f:H\to A$. Here an A∞ quasi-isomorphism is as defined in
[[def-a-infinity-morphism]]. In an explicit model whose underlying graded
space is identified with $H^*(A,m_1^A)$, the binary product is ordinarily
checked against the product induced by $m_2^A$; this definition does not
assert an existence or transfer theorem.

This is a definition of the data required for a minimal model. It does not
assert that every A∞-algebra has one or that a transfer theorem has been
proved.

Let $A$ and its cohomology groups be as in [[def-triple-massey-data]], and let
$\alpha\in H^p(A)$, $\beta\in H^q(A)$ and $\gamma\in H^r(A)$ be cohomology
classes. Their **triple Massey product** in that item's sign convention is the
subset

$$\langle\alpha,\beta,\gamma\rangle =\{[\omega(a,b,c;u,v)]\in H^{p+q+r-1}(A): (a,b,c;u,v)\text{ is a triple Massey datum representing }(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\}.$$

The expression is a cohomology class because it is closed by
[[lem-triple-massey-expression-is-closed]]. The set includes every choice of
cocycle representatives and null-homotopies for which the adjacent products
are boundaries; if there is no such datum, it is empty. No claim that the set
is a singleton is part of the definition.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]), and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be graded
$k$-vector spaces. A $k$-vector space is a unital left $k$-module as in
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. Tensor powers are formed using the tensor
products of
[[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]. If $f_i:V_i\to W_i$ are homogeneous
linear maps of degrees $d_i$, and $x_i\in V_i$ are homogeneous of degrees
$p_i$, the graded tensor map is defined on pure tensors by

$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{i>j}d_i p_j} f_1(x_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n(x_n).$$

It is extended linearly. In particular, for two maps,
$(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{|g||x|}f(x)\otimes g(y)$.

For homogeneous $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$, the
**Koszul sign** of reordering them to
$x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}$ is

$$\epsilon(\sigma;x_1,\ldots,x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{\substack{i<j\\\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)}} |x_{\sigma(i)}||x_{\sigma(j)}|}.$$

Thus swapping two adjacent homogeneous factors $x,y$ contributes
$(-1)^{|x||y|}$. Every tensor of maps, permutation, unshuffle, and symmetric
power below uses this same convention. A sign is a scalar in $k$ determined
only by the parity of the displayed integer exponent.

derivations.claim: The product is associative on triples involving the unit by the unit axiom. On nonunit basis elements, every nonzero pair product is one of $a,b,c$, each of which annihilates every nonunit. The only triple for which both adjacent pair-products are nonzero is $(x,y,z)$; both $(xy)z=az=0$ and $x(yz)=xb=0$. If just one adjacent pair-product is nonzero, the iterated product is zero whichever pair is multiplied first. Hence the bilinear product is associative.

The differential has degree $+1$: it sends $u,v$ of degree $-1$ to $a,b$ of degree zero and is zero on the other homogeneous basis elements. Since $d(a)=d(b)=0$, $d^2(u)=d^2(v)=0$, and $d^2$ is zero on every other basis element as well.

Define $f_1:H^*(A)\to A$ by the listed cocycle representatives, define $f_2([x],[y])=-u$ and $f_2([y],[z])=-v$, and set $f_2=0$ on all other basis pairs, in particular on pairs containing $[1_A]$. Put $f_n=0$ for $n\ge3$. The degrees are $|f_1|=0$ and $|f_2|=-1$, as required by [F5].

For the unit pairs, the signed Leibniz rule follows from $d(1_A)=0$. For the three nonzero nonunit products, both sides agree: $d(xy)=0=d(x)y+x\,d(y)$, $d(yz)=0=d(y)z+y\,d(z)$, and $d(xv)=0=d(x)v+x\,d(v)=xb$. If a nonunit product is zero and one factor is $u$ or $v$, its differential is $a$ or $b$, which annihilates every nonunit; the remaining term is zero because the other differential is zero. If neither factor is $u$ nor $v$, both differentials vanish. Thus the signed Leibniz rule holds on basis pairs and hence, by bilinearity, on all homogeneous elements.

The map $d:A^{-1}\to A^0$ sends $u\mapsto a$, $v\mapsto b$, and $c\mapsto0$. Its kernel is $kc$, its image is $k\{a,b\}$, and there is no degree $-2$ term. Also $d$ vanishes on $A^0$. Therefore $H^{-1}(A)=k[c]$, $H^0(A)=k[1_A]\oplus k[x]\oplus k[y]\oplus k[z]$, and all other cohomology groups are zero.
By steps 1.1, 1.2 and 2.1 the multiplication and differential satisfy every DGA axiom in [F1], so $A$ is a cohomological DGA. Its associated A∞-structure is the one of [F3].

The DGA product descends to these cohomology classes: replacing a degree-zero cycle by a boundary changes it by a multiple of $a$ or $b$, which multiplies every nonunit cycle to zero and multiplies the unit to a boundary; products involving $[c]$ and a nonunit cycle are zero. The unit acts as $[1_A]$. The only nonzero products among the chosen nonunit degree-zero representatives are $xy=a=du$ and $yz=b=dv$, so their classes are zero. Thus every product in the reduced cohomology span $k\{[x],[y],[z],[c]\}$ is zero.

The triple $(x,y,z;u,v)$ is valid Massey data because $xy=du=a$ and $yz=dv=b$. The fixed expression of [F7] is $-xv+uz=-c+0=-c$. Every representative of $[x]$, $[y]$, or $[z]$ differs from that basis vector by an element of $k\{a,b\}$. Their adjacent products remain $a$ and $b$, since $a,b$ annihilate nonunit basis elements. Every null-homotopy of $a$ is $u+\lambda c$ and every null-homotopy of $b$ is $v+\mu c$ for scalars $\lambda,\mu\in k$. All correction products involving $a,b,c$ in the expression vanish, so every datum representing these three classes gives $-c$. The triple Massey product is exactly $\{-[c]\}$.

On $H^*(A)$, take $m_1=0$ and let $m_2$ be the induced product. Define $m_3([x],[y],[z])=-[c]$, let $m_3$ be zero on every other ordered triple of the displayed basis, and set $m_n=0$ for $n\ge4$. The only nonzero value of $m_3$ has degree $0+0+0-1=-1$, as required by [F4].

The arity-one morphism identity says $d f_1=f_1m_1$, and both sides are zero because the chosen representatives are cycles. In arity two, the identity is $f_1m_2^H=d f_2+\mu(f_1\otimes f_1)$. On the pairs $([x],[y])$ and $([y],[z])$, its right side is respectively $-a+a=0$ and $-b+b=0$; on all other pairs of nonunit basis classes both terms are zero. If an input is $[1_A]$, $f_2$ is zero and $f_1$ preserves the unit, so the equality holds there too.

For arities $n=1,2$, the Stasheff sums vanish because $m_1=0$. For $n=3$, the identity is associativity of $m_2$: it holds on the unit by the unit law, and on three nonunit basis elements because their pairwise products are zero. Thus the identities hold through arity three.

In arity three, on $([x],[y],[z])$ the left side is $f_1m_3=-c$, and the right side is $\mu(f_1\otimes f_2)-\mu(f_2\otimes f_1) =x(-v)-(-u)z=-c$. On every other triple of nonunit basis classes both sides are zero: $m_3$ is zero there, and the only nonzero $f_2$ values have products $uz=0$ or $xv=c$ in precisely the triple already checked. If one input is the unit, the normalized condition $f_2(1_A,-)=f_2(-,1_A)=0$ makes the identity reduce to the unit law. For $(1_A,a,b)$ both sides equal $f_2(a,b)$; for $(a,1_A,b)$ both sides are zero; and for $(a,b,1_A)$ both sides equal $-f_2(a,b)$. With at least two units every $f_2$ term is zero.

In arity four, the only terms are insertions of $m_2$ into $m_3$ and of $m_3$ into $m_2$. derivations.claim: For a uniformly Cauchy sequence $T_m$ in $E$, each $T_m(c)$ is Cauchy in $C_B$, because $T_m-T_j\in F^pE$ eventually for every $p$. Define $T(c)=\lim_m T_m(c)$. Limits preserve addition, $B$-linearity, and each closed $F^qC_B$. Thus $T$ preserves the filtration and is continuous. If $T_m-T_j\in F^pE$ for all sufficiently large $j$, passing to the limit on every $F^qC_B$ gives $T_m-T\in F^pE$. More directly, a compatible family of cosets in $E/F^pE$ determines compatible evaluation cosets on each $c$ in every $C_B/F^nC_B$, without choosing simultaneous representatives. Their unique limit defines $T$; evaluating on $F^qC_B$ modulo $F^{p+q}$ proves that its class is the prescribed one in $E/F^pE$. This proves inverse-limit completeness as well; if $T\in\bigcap_pF^pE$, every $T(c)$ belongs to $\bigcap_pF^pC_B=0$, proving separation.

If $P\in F^pE$ and $Q\in F^qE$, then $PQ(F^rC_B)\subseteq P(F^{q+r}C_B)\subseteq F^{p+q+r}C_B$, proving multiplicativity. The coderivation equation, the counit equation, and evaluation at $1_C$ are closed conditions: reduce each equation modulo $F^n$ in its explicitly completed target, where sufficiently close maps agree. Consequently $\mathfrak l$ and every $F^p\mathfrak l$ are closed and complete in their induced filtration.

Put $p=|P|$, $q=|Q|$. For coderivations, the graded tensor composition rule gives $\Delta PQ=(PQ\otimes1+P\otimes Q+(-1)^{pq}Q\otimes P+1\otimes PQ)\Delta$. Subtracting $(-1)^{pq}\Delta QP$ cancels the two mixed terms and gives $\Delta[P,Q]=([P,Q]\otimes1+1\otimes[P,Q])\Delta$. Also $[P,Q](1_C)=0$ and $\epsilon[P,Q]=0$. Thus coderivations are closed under the commutator, and multiplicativity proves the additive filtration bound.

The commutator is graded skew because $[P,Q]=-(-1)^{pq}[Q,P]$. For $|R|=r$, direct expansion of $[P,[Q,R]]$ is $PQR-(-1)^{qr}PRQ-(-1)^{p(q+r)}QRP+(-1)^{p(q+r)+qr}RQP$. The expansion of $\bigl[ [P,Q],R\bigr]$ is $PQR-(-1)^{pq}QPR-(-1)^{(p+q)r}RPQ+(-1)^{(p+q)r+pq}RQP$. The expansion of $(-1)^{pq}[Q,[P,R]]$ is $(-1)^{pq}QPR-(-1)^{pq+pr}QRP-(-1)^{qr}PRQ+(-1)^{qr+pr}RPQ$. The $QPR$ and $RPQ$ terms cancel in the last two expressions; the other four agree with the first expression. This proves the graded Jacobi identity in derivation form, with all signs explicit.

For homogeneous $T$ of degree $t$, expanding $[D,[D,T]]$ gives $D^2T-TD^2$, since the two $DTD$ terms have coefficients $-(-1)^t$ and $+(-1)^t$. Hence $d^2T=0$. Substituting $P=D$ into the Jacobi identity proved in step 4.1 gives $d[P,Q]=[dP,Q]+(-1)^{|P|}[P,dQ]$. Because $D$ preserves each coefficient filtration, composition with $D$ and hence $d$ preserve every $F^pE$ and every $F^p\mathfrak l$.

The preceding steps prove all graded Lie, differential, completeness, and filtration axioms on $F^1\mathfrak l$. In each quotient by $F^n$, any bracket with at least $n$ positive-order entries vanishes by the additive bound. Thus the positive filtration is pronilpotent as well as complete, as claimed.

Let $k$ be a characteristic-zero field, let $B$ be a commutative unital $k$-algebra concentrated in degree zero, and let $I$ be an ideal such that $B\cong\varprojlim_{n\ge1}B/I^n$. Nilpotent ideals are included. Let $V$ be any graded $k$-vector space; no finite-dimensionality assumption is made. Use the graded tensor convention of [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]].

The carrier $C$ is either the coaugmented tensor coalgebra $T^c(V)=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}V^{\otimes r}$ with deconcatenation, or the coaugmented graded symmetric coalgebra $S^c(V)=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}S^r(V)$ with unshuffle coproduct. For the latter, $S^r$ means graded symmetric coinvariants, and the coproduct sums over all divisions of the inputs into two ordered sublists, with the Koszul sign. The empty word is $1_C$, the counit $\epsilon$ is projection to length zero, and the coaugmentation is inclusion of scalars. These formulas specify the carrier without requiring a cofree universal property.

Define its coefficient completion, filtration, and tensor target by

$$C_B=\varprojlim_n(C\otimes_k B/I^n),\qquad F^nC_B=\ker(C_B\longrightarrow C\otimes_k B/I^n),\qquad F^0C_B=C_B.$$

$$C_B\widehat\otimes_B C_B=\varprojlim_n((C\otimes_k C)\otimes_k B/I^n).$$

All structure maps are extended through these inverse limits. This is coefficient completion of a direct sum: modulo each $I^n$ every element has finite length support. No unrestricted product over arities is included. Completed tensor powers and polynomial coefficients mean the analogous explicit inverse limits. A homogeneous map is understood in the grading induced by $C$, and continuity always means the displayed coefficient topology.

Let $E$ be the graded composition algebra of continuous $B$-linear filtration-preserving endomorphisms of $C_B$. Its order filtration is

$$F^pE=\{T:T(F^qC_B)\subseteq F^{p+q}C_B\text{ for every }q\ge0\}\quad(p\ge0).$$

Let $\mathfrak l\subset E$ be the homogeneous coderivations satisfying $T(1_C)=0$, $\epsilon T=0$, and

$$\Delta T=(T\otimes1+1\otimes T)\Delta.$$

The sign in $1\otimes T$ is the graded tensor sign. In particular these coderivations have zero nullary component. Fix $D\in\mathfrak l^1$ with $D^2=0$. A **coefficient-complete fixed-carrier codifferential deformation** is $D+R$ with $R\in F^1\mathfrak l^1$ and $(D+R)^2=0$. Its allowed equivalences are degree-zero continuous $B$-linear counital coaugmented coalgebra automorphisms $G$ such that $G-\operatorname{id}\in F^1E$, acting by $D+R\mapsto G(D+R)G^{-1}$.

Here identity modulo $I$ can equivalently be stated as $(G-\operatorname{id})(C_B)\subseteq F^1C_B$. To see the filtration implication without assuming that $I$ is finitely generated, observe that $F^qC_B$ is the closure of $C\otimes I^q$: modulo $F^n$, $n>q$, every element lifts from $C\otimes I^q$. By $B$-linearity a continuous map with image in $F^1$ carries that dense submodule into $F^{q+1}$; closedness gives the same inclusion on all $F^q$.

This contract uses all continuous coefficient-complete Taylor operations. It does not identify them with a naive algebraic tensor $\operatorname{Hom}_k(W,U)\otimes I$ when the coefficient algebra is infinite dimensional. Over a finite-dimensional coefficient algebra, expanding in a finite coefficient basis does give the usual tensor identification, without any finite-dimensionality assumption on $W,U$.

derivations.claim: The terms $X^j$ and $N^j$ belong to $F^jE$. Therefore all displayed series have finite reductions modulo every $F^nE$ and define unique limits. Multiplication respects these limits because the filtration is multiplicative. In particular any one-variable formal series with rational coefficients and zero-order constant defined in $k$ can be evaluated at a positive-order element: each coefficient calculation becomes finite in every quotient.

In $\mathbb Q[\![t]\!]$, define $\ell(t)=\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^{j-1}t^j/j$. Termwise differentiation gives $\ell'(t)=(1+t)^{-1}$. The formal chain rule, obtained by expanding products coefficient by coefficient, gives $h'=h/(1+t)$ for $h=\exp\ell(t)$ and $h(0)=1$. From $(1+t)h'=h$ the coefficient recursion gives $h=1+t$: its coefficient of $t$ is $1$ and every higher coefficient is zero. Also the formal derivative of $\ell(\exp(t)-1)$ is $1$ and its constant coefficient is zero, so $\ell(\exp(t)-1)=t$. Each assertion is an identity of scalar coefficient series.

Induction on $r$ proves $(\operatorname{ad}_X)^r(T)=\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j\binom rjX^{r-j}TX^j$: the induction step multiplies once on the left and subtracts once on the right, and Pascal's identity collects the overlapping terms. Every summand has filtration order at least $r$, even if $T$ has order zero, so the resulting exponential series converges.

Substitute $N$ and $X$ into the two scalar identities modulo $F^nE$ and pass to the inverse limit, using step 1.1. This proves $\exp(\log(1+N))=1+N$ and $\log(\exp X)=X$. The substitution is sound in the noncommutative algebra because every identity involves powers of one fixed element only. The coefficient of total degree $r>0$ in $\exp(X)\exp(-X)$ is $X^r\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^j/(j!(r-j)!)=0$; the degree-zero coefficient is $1$. Thus the exponential inverse is $\exp(-X)$ and both inverse bijections have the stated domains.

Expanding $\exp(X)T\exp(-X)$ modulo $F^nE$ and collecting the terms containing a total of $r$ copies of $X$ gives $\sum_{j=0}^r(-1)^jX^{r-j}TX^j/((r-j)!j!)=(\operatorname{ad}_X)^r(T)/r!$. Passing to limits gives the conjugation identity. If $E$ is graded and $|X|=0$, its graded commutator with $T$ is exactly the ordinary commutator used here, so the same proof applies in every homogeneous degree.

derivations.claim: Applying [F3] to the composite tensor maps gives $u_A^{\otimes n}s_A^{\otimes n}=(-1)^{c_n}\operatorname{id}$ and $s_A^{\otimes n}u_A^{\otimes n}=(-1)^{c_n}\operatorname{id}$. Thus the displayed formulas for $m_n$ and $b_n$ are mutually inverse. The degree of $b_n$ is $-1+(2-n)+n=1$. On inputs $s_Aa_j$ the tensor map $u_A^{\otimes n}$ contributes exponent $\sum_j(n-j)(|a_j|-1)$; adding $c_n=\sum_j(n-j)$ gives the stated evaluation formula. For $F_n$ exactly the same computation gives degree zero, inverse $f_n=u_D F_n s_A^{\otimes n}$, and evaluation $F_n(s_Aa_1,\ldots,s_Aa_n)=(-1)^{\sum_j(n-j)|a_j|}s_Df_n(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$.

More generally any degree-$d$ maps $v_n:X^{\otimes n}\to X$ extend by the consecutive insertion formula $V(1)=0$, $V(x_1\cdots x_N)=\sum_{r+s+t=N}(-1)^{d\sum_{j\le r}|x_j|}x_1\cdots x_r v_s(x_{r+1},\ldots,x_{r+s})x_{r+s+1}\cdots x_N$. It is finite on every word, has zero counit, and satisfies $\Delta V=(V\otimes1+1\otimes V)\Delta$. Indeed a cut of the output word is either before or after the single replaced block. These choices correspond respectively to acting on the suffix or prefix at the corresponding cut of the input word; the Koszul sign on $1\otimes V$ accounts for moving $V$ across the prefix. Coaugmentation terms satisfy the same equation because $V(1)=0$.

These extensions are unique. For a coderivation with zero counit and zero corestrictions, assume inductively it vanishes on shorter nonempty words. Its coderivation identity on a word of length $N$ then says that its value has zero reduced coproduct, so is primitive. In a tensor coalgebra with zero scalar part, a primitive lies in $X$: for each component of length $j>1$, the reduced coproduct component $X\otimes X^{\otimes(j-1)}$ is the canonical injective splitting of that component, hence cannot vanish unless it does. The primitive value has zero length-one projection by the corestriction hypothesis, hence is zero. This proves the induction, starting at length one. In particular the insertion extension defines the asserted unique $B$ without any cofree assertion left unproved.

Fix $r+s+t=N$, put $k=r+1+t$, and compare one projected term with $s_A m_k(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t})u_A^{\otimes N}$. Evaluating on $s_Aa_1,\ldots,s_Aa_N$ by [F3] cancels all input-dependent sign differences: the inner insertion on suspended inputs contributes $\sum_{j\le r}(|a_j|-1)$, the inner tensor of $u_A$ contributes $\sum_{j=1}^s(s-j)(|a_{r+j}|-1)$, and the outer tensor of $u_A$ uses the middle unsuspended output degree $\sum_{j=1}^s|a_{r+j}|+2-s$ with coefficient $t$. On the comparison map the corresponding input insertion sign is $(2-s)\sum_{j\le r}|a_j|$ after applying $u_A^{\otimes N}$. Subtracting these exponents leaves the input-independent difference $D=-r-c_s-c_k+t(2-s)+c_N$, in addition to the prefactor $c_s+c_k$ from the two $b$ maps. Hence the total difference is $c_N-r+t(2-s)$, congruent to $c_N+r+st$ modulo two. We have proved in every arity the exact map identity $b_k(1^{\otimes r}\otimes b_s\otimes1^{\otimes t})=(-1)^{c_N+r+st}s_A m_k(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t})u_A^{\otimes N}$.

On the right write $p_j=i_1+\cdots+i_{j-1}$, and evaluate a fixed block term on $s_Aa_1,\ldots,s_Aa_N$. The suspended coefficient has exponent $E=\sum_j\sum_{\ell=1}^{i_j}(i_j-\ell)|a_{p_j+\ell}|+\sum_j(q-j)(\sum_{\ell=1}^{i_j}|a_{p_j+\ell}|+1-i_j)$, by step 1.1 applied first to the $F$ blocks and then to $b_q^D$. The comparison map $s_Dm_q^D(f_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{i_q})u_A^{\otimes N}$ has exponent $E'=\sum_{h=1}^N(N-h)|a_h|-c_N+\sum_j(1-i_j)\sum_{h\le p_j}|a_h|$. For the input in position $p_j+\ell$, both exponents have coefficient $i_j-\ell+q-j$; this follows in $E'$ by replacing the remaining tail length with $\sum_{v>j}i_v$. Their difference is thus $E-E'=c_N+\sum_j(q-j)(1-i_j)$, congruent to $c_N+\eta(i_1,\ldots,i_q)$. This proves $b_q^D(F_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{i_q})=(-1)^{c_N+\eta}s_Dm_q^D(f_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{i_q})u_A^{\otimes N}$.

The square of a degree-one coderivation is again a coderivation: expand $(B\otimes1+1\otimes B)^2$ and use [F3]; the mixed terms are $B\otimes B$ and $-B\otimes B$ and cancel over any field. It has zero counit and vanishes on $1$. Its length-one projection on $X^{\otimes N}$ is therefore $\sum_{r+s+t=N}b_{r+1+t}(1^{\otimes r}\otimes b_s\otimes1^{\otimes t})$. By uniqueness from step 2.1, $B^2=0$ is equivalent to the vanishing of all these projections.

For degree-zero corestrictions $F_n$ define $F(1)=1$ and $F(x_1\cdots x_N)=\sum_{q=1}^N\sum_{i_1+\cdots+i_q=N,\ i_j\ge1}F_{i_1}(x_1,\ldots,x_{i_1})\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{i_q}(x_{N-i_q+1},\ldots,x_N)$. There is no factorial because blocks are consecutive and ordered. A deconcatenation cut of this output is between two output blocks, and corresponds to a cut of the input together with consecutive partitions of its two pieces. Therefore $\Delta F=(F\otimes F)\Delta$; no additional map-interchange sign occurs because the $F_n$ have degree zero. This defines a counit- and coaugmentation-preserving coalgebra map. Uniqueness follows by induction on input length: two maps agreeing on shorter words and on their corestrictions have primitive difference on the next word, and step 2.1 makes that difference zero.

On the left, the sign calculation of step 2.2 is unchanged when the outer $m_k$ is replaced by $f_k$: that calculation uses the degree $2-s$ of the inner operation, and its outer input degrees, not the degree of the outer operation. It gives $F_k(1^{\otimes r}\otimes b_s^A\otimes1^{\otimes t})=(-1)^{c_N+r+st}s_D f_k(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s^A\otimes1^{\otimes t})u_A^{\otimes N}$.

Summing the identity of step 2.2 factors out the invertible outer maps $s_A,u_A^{\otimes N}$ and the common sign $(-1)^{c_N}$. The resulting equation is exactly [F1]. Steps 1.1 and 3.1 thus prove both implications and the structure bijection, with no characteristic restriction or division. All the insertion and uniqueness arguments restrict to the reduced coalgebra, and extending a reduced coderivation by zero on $1$ recovers its unique counital coaugmented version. This proves the structure assertion, including the absence of nullary terms.

The map $D_F=FB_A-B_DF$ vanishes on $1$, has zero counit, and obeys $\Delta D_F=(D_F\otimes F+F\otimes D_F)\Delta$. This follows by expanding the coderivation and coalgebra-map identities, using degree zero for $F$. If all length-one corestrictions of $D_F$ vanish, induction on input length makes all its values primitive and then zero, exactly as in step 2.1. Consequently $FB_A=B_DF$ is equivalent to equality of their length-one projections in every arity. The left projection is $\sum_{r+s+t=N}F_k(1^{\otimes r}\otimes b_s^A\otimes1^{\otimes t})$ and the right is $\sum_{q,\ i_1+\cdots+i_q=N}b_q^D(F_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{i_q})$.

Equating the two projections from step 4.2 and substituting the two sign comparisons cancels their common invertible maps and sign $(-1)^{c_N}$. What remains is precisely [F2], including its actual right-hand exponent $\eta$. Conversely those identities give zero projections, hence the full coalgebra equation by step 4.2. The coefficient transformations in step 1.1 are invertible, and step 3.2 gives unique coalgebra extensions, so this is a bijection on the native morphisms as asserted.

For a second family $g$ the length-one projection of $GF$ is the sum of $G_q(F_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes F_{i_q})$. The sign calculation of step 2.3 only uses the degrees $1-i_j$ of the inner $f$ maps and the input evaluation formula for the outer suspended map. Replacing the outer $m_q^D$ by $g_q$ therefore gives the same sign $c_N+\eta$. Desuspending by the inverse transformation from step 1.1 yields the stated composition coefficients. The identity coalgebra map has only $F_1=\operatorname{id}$, which desuspends to $f_1=\operatorname{id}$ and $f_n=0$ for $n>1$. Finally the explicit arity-one and arity-two formulas follow from $c_1=0,c_2=1$; the degree of $s_Aa$ makes the binary evaluation sign $(-1)^{|a|}$. Simultaneously negating all coderivation coefficients negates $B$, so leaves $B^2=0$ and $FB_A=B_DF$ unchanged when done on both sides. This establishes all sign and compatibility claims.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]) and let
$A=\bigoplus_{j\in\mathbb Z}A^j$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded $k$-vector space; its tensor
maps use the convention in [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]]. An
**uncurved cohomological A∞-algebra in the unsuspended convention** is a
sequence of homogeneous $k$-linear maps

$$m_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow A,\qquad |m_n|=2-n, \qquad n\ge1,$$

such that for every $n\ge1$ the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to A$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st} m_{r+1+t}\bigl(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s\otimes1^{\otimes t}\bigr)=0.$$

Here $1$ denotes the identity map of $A$, the tensor maps use the Koszul rule,
and the displayed sign $(-1)^{r+st}$ is part of the fixed convention. The
degree condition means that for homogeneous inputs of degrees $j_1,\ldots,j_n$,
$m_n$ has output degree $j_1+\cdots+j_n+2-n$.

“Uncurved” means no arity-zero operation $m_0$ is included. “Nonunital” means
that no unit is part of this definition. A unit or a strict-unit condition on
higher operations is additional data and must be stated separately. No graded
commutativity is assumed for $m_2$.

Let $A$ and $B$ be uncurved cohomological A∞-algebras in the convention of
[[def-a-infinity-algebra]]. An **A∞-morphism** $f:A\to B$ is a family of
homogeneous maps

$$f_n:A^{\otimes_k n}\longrightarrow B,\qquad |f_n|=1-n,\qquad n\ge1,$$

such that, for every $n\ge1$, the following equality of maps
$A^{\otimes_k n}\to B$ holds:

$$\sum_{\substack{r,s,t\ge0,\ s\ge1\\r+s+t=n}} (-1)^{r+st}f_{r+1+t}(1^{\otimes r}\otimes m_s^A\otimes1^{\otimes t}) =\sum_{q=1}^{n}\ \sum_{\substack{i_1+\cdots+i_q=n\\i_j\ge1}} (-1)^{\eta(i_1,\ldots,i_q)} m_q^B(f_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes f_{i_q}),$$

where
$\eta(i_1,\ldots,i_q)=\sum_{j=1}^{q-1}(q-j)(i_j-1)$ and all tensor maps
use [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]]. The identity at $n=1$ says
that $f_1$ is a cochain map from $(A,m_1^A)$ to $(B,m_1^B)$.

An A∞-morphism is an **A∞ quasi-isomorphism** if $f_1$ induces an isomorphism
on cohomology, where
$H^j(A,m_1^A)=\ker(m_1^A:A^j\to A^{j+1})/\operatorname{im}(m_1^A:A^{j-1}\to A^j)$
and likewise for $B$. This definition imposes no unit condition on $f$.

Let $k$ be a field ([[def-field]]), and let $V_1,\ldots,V_n$ be graded
$k$-vector spaces. A $k$-vector space is a unital left $k$-module as in
[[def-left-and-right-modules]]. Tensor powers are formed using the tensor
products of
[[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]. If $f_i:V_i\to W_i$ are homogeneous
linear maps of degrees $d_i$, and $x_i\in V_i$ are homogeneous of degrees
$p_i$, the graded tensor map is defined on pure tensors by

$$(f_1\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n)(x_1\otimes\cdots\otimes x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{i>j}d_i p_j} f_1(x_1)\otimes\cdots\otimes f_n(x_n).$$

It is extended linearly. In particular, for two maps,
$(f\otimes g)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{|g||x|}f(x)\otimes g(y)$.

For homogeneous $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ and a permutation $\sigma\in S_n$, the
**Koszul sign** of reordering them to
$x_{\sigma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{\sigma(n)}$ is

$$\epsilon(\sigma;x_1,\ldots,x_n) =(-1)^{\sum_{\substack{i<j\\\sigma(i)>\sigma(j)}} |x_{\sigma(i)}||x_{\sigma(j)}|}.$$

Thus swapping two adjacent homogeneous factors $x,y$ contributes
$(-1)^{|x||y|}$. Every tensor of maps, permutation, unshuffle, and symmetric
power below uses this same convention. A sign is a scalar in $k$ determined
only by the parity of the displayed integer exponent.

derivations.claim: The complete filtered endomorphism algebra and its closed coderivation subspace are supplied by [[lem-complete-coderivations-form-a-filtered-differential-graded-lie-algebra]]. Thus [[lem-noncommutative-filtered-exponential-and-logarithm]] defines inverse exponential and logarithm series on positive-order degree-zero endomorphisms. All subsequent identities can be checked in $C_n=C\otimes_k B/I^n$ and its tensor target and then passed to limits.

Conversely, let $G$ be allowed and $N=G-\operatorname{id}$. On $C_n$, $N^n=0$. Define the endomorphism-valued polynomial $P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom tjN^j$. For every nonnegative integer $m$, the finite binomial theorem gives $P_n(m)=G^m$. Since $G^m$ is a counital coaugmented coalgebra map, $\Delta P_n(m)=(P_n(m)\otimes P_n(m))\Delta$, $P_n(m)(1_C)=1_C$, and $\epsilon P_n(m)=\epsilon$.

For $X\in F^1\mathfrak l^0$, induction on $j$ using its coderivation equation gives $\Delta X^j=(X\otimes1+1\otimes X)^j\Delta$. The operators $X\otimes1$ and $1\otimes X$ commute because $X$ has degree zero. Each is of positive coefficient order, so the exponential and binomial calculations are finite in each quotient. Consequently $\Delta\exp X=(\exp X\otimes\exp X)\Delta$. Also $\exp X(1_C)=1_C$ and $\epsilon\exp X=\epsilon$, because every positive power of $X$ kills $1_C$ and is killed by $\epsilon$. Its inverse $\exp(-X)$ has the same properties. Hence exponential gives an allowed automorphism.

Each difference in these three identities is a polynomial in $t$ with coefficients in a $k$-vector space of maps. A polynomial of degree at most $a$ with such coefficients vanishing at $a+1$ distinct nonnegative integers has zero coefficients: apply the inverse of their scalar Vandermonde matrix over the characteristic-zero field $k$. This does not require finite-dimensional map spaces or any domain property of $B/I^n$. Therefore the identities of step 1.2 hold as polynomial identities for the indeterminate $t$.

Differentiate those polynomial identities at $t=0$. Since $P_n(0)=\operatorname{id}$, the result is $\Delta P_n'(0)=(P_n'(0)\otimes1+1\otimes P_n'(0))\Delta$, $P_n'(0)(1_C)=0$, and $\epsilon P_n'(0)=0$. For $j\ge1$, differentiation of $t(t-1)\cdots(t-j+1)/j!$ at zero gives $(-1)^{j-1}/j$. Thus $P_n'(0)=\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(-1)^{j-1}N^j/j$, exactly the reduction of $\log G$.

These reductions are compatible for all $n$, and the coderivation, counit, and coaugmentation identities are closed in the completed targets. Therefore $\log G\in F^1\mathfrak l^0$. Step 1.1 gives inverse identities for the underlying endomorphisms, and step 2.1 shows that every positive-order degree-zero coderivation exponentiates into the allowed group. The restrictions are therefore mutually inverse bijections onto the entire stated group.

citations.quote:
Use [[def-coefficient-complete-codifferential-deformation]]. The order filtration on $E$ is separated and complete, with $F^pE\,F^qE\subseteq F^{p+q}E$. The coderivations form a closed graded Lie subalgebra for

$$[P,Q]=PQ-(-1)^{|P||Q|}QP.$$

With $dT=[D,T]$, the positive-order space $\mathfrak g=F^1\mathfrak l$ is a complete filtered differential graded Lie algebra, with $F^p\mathfrak g=F^p\mathfrak l$ for $p\ge1$, $d(F^p\mathfrak g)\subseteq F^p\mathfrak g$, and $[F^p\mathfrak g,F^q\mathfrak g]\subseteq F^{p+q}\mathfrak g$.

Let $E$ be any unital associative $k$-algebra over a characteristic-zero field, with descending two-sided filtration $F^0E=E$, $F^pE\,F^qE\subseteq F^{p+q}E$, and $E\cong\varprojlim E/F^nE$. Commutativity is not assumed. The formulas

$$\exp X=\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{X^j}{j!},\qquad \log(1+N)=\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{(-1)^{j-1}N^j}{j}$$

give mutually inverse bijections $F^1E\leftrightarrow1+F^1E$, and $\exp(-X)$ is the inverse of $\exp X$. For $X\in F^1E$ and $T\in E$,

$$\exp(X)T\exp(-X)=\sum_{r\ge0}\frac{(\operatorname{ad}_X)^r(T)}{r!},\qquad \operatorname{ad}_X(T)=XT-TX.$$

The same conclusions apply to degree-zero $X$ in a graded algebra; $T$ may have any homogeneous degree. In particular they apply to the complete endomorphism algebra in [[def-coefficient-complete-codifferential-deformation]] once its completeness is established.

Let $k$ be a characteristic-zero field, let $B$ be a commutative unital $k$-algebra concentrated in degree zero, and let $I$ be an ideal such that $B\cong\varprojlim_{n\ge1}B/I^n$. Nilpotent ideals are included. Let $V$ be any graded $k$-vector space; no finite-dimensionality assumption is made. Use the graded tensor convention of [[def-koszul-sign-rule-for-graded-tensors]].

The carrier $C$ is either the coaugmented tensor coalgebra $T^c(V)=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}V^{\otimes r}$ with deconcatenation, or the coaugmented graded symmetric coalgebra $S^c(V)=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}S^r(V)$ with unshuffle coproduct. For the latter, $S^r$ means graded symmetric coinvariants, and the coproduct sums over all divisions of the inputs into two ordered sublists, with the Koszul sign. The empty word is $1_C$, the counit $\epsilon$ is projection to length zero, and the coaugmentation is inclusion of scalars. These formulas specify the carrier without requiring a cofree universal property.

Define its coefficient completion, filtration, and tensor target by

$$C_B=\varprojlim_n(C\otimes_k B/I^n),\qquad F^nC_B=\ker(C_B\longrightarrow C\otimes_k B/I^n),\qquad F^0C_B=C_B.$$

$$C_B\widehat\otimes_B C_B=\varprojlim_n((C\otimes_k C)\otimes_k B/I^n).$$

All structure maps are extended through these inverse limits. This is coefficient completion of a direct sum: modulo each $I^n$ every element has finite length support. No unrestricted product over arities is included. Completed tensor powers and polynomial coefficients mean the analogous explicit inverse limits. A homogeneous map is understood in the grading induced by $C$, and continuity always means the displayed coefficient topology.

Let $E$ be the graded composition algebra of continuous $B$-linear filtration-preserving endomorphisms of $C_B$. Its order filtration is

$$F^pE=\{T:T(F^qC_B)\subseteq F^{p+q}C_B\text{ for every }q\ge0\}\quad(p\ge0).$$

Let $\mathfrak l\subset E$ be the homogeneous coderivations satisfying $T(1_C)=0$, $\epsilon T=0$, and

$$\Delta T=(T\otimes1+1\otimes T)\Delta.$$

The sign in $1\otimes T$ is the graded tensor sign. In particular these coderivations have zero nullary component. Fix $D\in\mathfrak l^1$ with $D^2=0$. A **coefficient-complete fixed-carrier codifferential deformation** is $D+R$ with $R\in F^1\mathfrak l^1$ and $(D+R)^2=0$. Its allowed equivalences are degree-zero continuous $B$-linear counital coaugmented coalgebra automorphisms $G$ such that $G-\operatorname{id}\in F^1E$, acting by $D+R\mapsto G(D+R)G^{-1}$.

Here identity modulo $I$ can equivalently be stated as $(G-\operatorname{id})(C_B)\subseteq F^1C_B$. To see the filtration implication without assuming that $I$ is finitely generated, observe that $F^qC_B$ is the closure of $C\otimes I^q$: modulo $F^n$, $n>q$, every element lifts from $C\otimes I^q$. By $B$-linearity a continuous map with image in $F^1$ carries that dense submodule into $F^{q+1}$; closedness gives the same inclusion on all $F^q$.

This contract uses all continuous coefficient-complete Taylor operations. It does not identify them with a naive algebraic tensor $\operatorname{Hom}_k(W,U)\otimes I$ when the coefficient algebra is infinite dimensional. Over a finite-dimensional coefficient algebra, expanding in a finite coefficient basis does give the usual tensor identification, without any finite-dimensionality assumption on $W,U$.

derivations.claim: The ideal $P=F^1W$ is complete and separated for its induced filtration: a compatible family of elements of $P/F^NW$ defines a compatible family in $W/F^NW$, whose unique lift lies in the kernel of $W\to W/F^1W$, namely $P$. The same argument applies degreewise and to $P'$. Products and coproducts preserve total weight: for a product weights add, and a split of a monomial preserves the sum of the two output weights. They therefore extend to the inverse limits and their completed tensor targets, retaining the algebra and coalgebra identities since these hold on the dense uncompleted subspaces. Scalars, the counit and the coaugmentation extend as well. The length-one projection takes $\mathcal F^NC(P)$ into $F^NW$, so it extends to $P$.

On $C(P)$ the coderivation formula is $Q(1)=0$ and $Q(x_1\cdots x_m)=\sum_{\varnothing\ne I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}}\epsilon(I,I^c;x)q_{|I|}(x_I)x_{I^c}$. Each term has at least the input's total weight by the bound on $q_{|I|}$. Thus $Q$ is continuous and extends. The coderivation identity can be checked by selecting the nonempty distinguished block acted on by $q$ and distributing all remaining factors to the two coproduct outputs; both sides make precisely these selections. The Koszul signs agree, including the sign from moving the degree-one $Q$ across the left output when it acts on the right output. The given $Q^2=0$ continues to hold by density and continuity.

The partition formula for $F$ is finite on each monomial and preserves its total weight. In $\Delta F$, split the output blocks between the two tensor factors. In $(F\otimes F)\Delta$, first split the inputs into the unions of those two groups and then partition each union. These choices are in bijection; the binomial number of ways of splitting ordered output blocks changes $1/s!$ to the product of the two output factorial coefficients. Both signs implement the same permutation of input factors. This proves the coalgebra identity directly and shows that the length-one corestrictions are exactly $f_n$. The finite coalgebra map is determined uniquely by these corestrictions: induct on input length, subtract two such maps and use the reduced coproduct; their difference on the next input has zero reduced coproduct and hence is primitive, so lies in the length-one summand, where its projection is zero. The primitive assertion is exactly [F2], whose proof composes the singleton coproduct component with multiplication to give $s$ times the identity on length $s>1$; characteristic zero makes that coefficient invertible. The weight bound extends $F$ continuously, and $FQ=RF$ extends from the dense subspace. Uniqueness of each continuous extension follows from separatedness of the target.

The term $w^n/n!$ has total weight at least $n$, and each of $q_n(w^n)/n!$ and $f_n(w^n)/n!$ lies in filtration $n$. All three series therefore stabilize modulo every filtration quotient and converge uniquely. The series with marked input $v$ has its $n$th coefficient in filtration $p+n$. In characteristic zero the factorials are invertible. Every reordering of these sums is finite modulo total weight $N$, so it is legitimate in the inverse limit. The binomial coproduct expansion gives $\Delta e^w=e^w\otimes e^w$, and the binomial multiplication expansion gives $e^we^{-w}=1$.

In $Q(w^m)$ the choice of a distinguished block of size $i$ has multiplicity $m!/(i!(m-i)!)$. As $w$ has degree zero all such signs are positive. Divide by $m!$ and sum to obtain $Q(e^w)=(\sum_{i\ge1}q_i(w^i)/i!)e^w=c_q(w)e^w$. For $F(w^m)$, an ordered partition of block sizes $i_1,\ldots,i_s$ occurs $m!/(i_1!\cdots i_s!)$ times. Summing its partition formula after division by $m!$ gives $F(e^w)=\sum_{s\ge0}(1/s!)(\sum_{i\ge1}f_i(w^i)/i!)^s=e^u$.

To evaluate $F(ve^w)$ distinguish the unique output block containing $v$. Choose its $n$ unmarked inputs and apply $f_{n+1}(w^n,v)$; the sum over partitions of all remaining inputs is $e^u$ by step 5.1. The factorials reduce to $1/n!$ on the marked block and the usual output factorial on the other blocks. Moving $v$ or the marked output past copies of the degree-zero $w$ or $u$ produces no signs. This gives the stated marked-input identity, with convergence from step 4.1, and completes all assertions.

citations.quote:
Let $W=V[1]$ and $Z=U[1]$ be the shifted spaces of two complete filtered L∞-algebras over the same characteristic-zero field, in the convention of [[def-complete-filtered-l-infinity-algebra]]. Write $Q,R$ for their degree-one square-zero coderivations and $q_n,r_n$ for their corestrictions. A **filtered L∞-morphism** from $W$ to $Z$ consists of degree-zero graded symmetric maps $f_n:S^nW\to Z$, $n\ge1$, with

$$f_n(F^{i_1}W,\ldots,F^{i_n}W)\subseteq F^{i_1+\cdots+i_n}Z\qquad(i_j\ge1),$$

whose associated coaugmented coalgebra map $F:k\oplus S^c(W)\to k\oplus S^c(Z)$ satisfies $FQ=RF$, after extending $Q,R$ by $Q(1)=R(1)=0$. There is no constant Taylor coefficient: $F(1)=1$. Explicitly, for homogeneous inputs,

$$F(x_1\cdots x_n)=\sum_{s=1}^n\frac1{s!}\sum_{(B_1,\ldots,B_s)}\epsilon(B_1,\ldots,B_s;x)\,f_{|B_1|}(x_{B_1})\cdots f_{|B_s|}(x_{B_s}).$$

The inner sum runs over ordered partitions of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ into nonempty blocks. Inside each block retain the original input order; $\epsilon$ is the Koszul sign of the permutation which lists those blocks in the indicated order. The factor $1/s!$ removes ordering of the graded symmetric output blocks. The length-one projection of $F$ on $S^nW$ is $f_n$.

The composite of $f:W\to Z$ and $g:Z\to T$ has associated map $GF$; its Taylor coefficients are the length-one projections of $GF$. The identity has $f_1=\operatorname{id}$ and $f_n=0$ for $n>1$. These definitions do not require $F^1W=W$. The complete positive ideal $P=F^1W$ is the space on which completed exponentials and Maurer–Cartan sums will be used.

Let $S^c(W)$ and $\bar\Delta$ be as in
[[def-reduced-graded-symmetric-coalgebra]]. The reduced coproduct is
well-defined on the graded-symmetric quotient, is coassociative and
graded-cocommutative, and is conilpotent: every element is killed by a
sufficiently long iterated reduced coproduct. Its primitive subspace
($\ker\bar\Delta$) is exactly $S^1(W)=W$.

derivations.claim: The series defining $u=f_*(w)$ converges in $F^1Z^0$ by [F1]. Since $FQ=RF$, its exponential satisfies $c_r(u)e^u=R(e^u)=RF(e^w)=FQ(e^w)=F(c_q(w)e^w)$. The marked-input identity of [F1] rewrites the last expression as $(\sum_{n\ge0}f_{n+1}(w^n,c_q(w))/n!)e^u$. Multiply by $e^{-u}$ to obtain the curvature formula. This series converges since its $n$th term has filtration at least $n+1$.

The continuous coalgebra map $GF$ intertwines coderivations because $GFQ=GRF=S GF$, where $S$ is the coderivation on $T$. Its length-one projection on $S^nW$ applies $g_s$ to the length-$s$ part of the partition formula for $F$, giving exactly the stated formula for $h_n$. Every term has degree zero and additive filtration, because first the $f$ blocks and then $g_s$ add the input filtration indices. Thus $h$ is a filtered morphism.

If $c_q(w)=0$, every term on the right vanishes, so $c_r(f_*(w))=0$ and [F2] gives the asserted map on Maurer–Cartan elements. For $w-v\in F^pW$ with $w,v\in F^1W^0$, the multilinear telescoping expansion of $f_n(w^n)-f_n(v^n)$ has in every term one input in $F^pW$ and all other inputs in $F^1W$, so it lies in $F^{p+n-1}Z$. Hence $f_*(w)-f_*(v)\in F^pZ$. This proves continuity in the filtration topology.

For repeated degree-zero $w$, the coefficient formula becomes $h_n(w^n)=\sum_{s=1}^n(1/s!)\sum_{i_1+\cdots+i_s=n,\ i_j\ge1}(n!/(i_1!\cdots i_s!))g_s(f_{i_1}(w^{i_1}),\ldots,f_{i_s}(w^{i_s}))$. After dividing by $n!$ and summing over $n$, the result is $\sum_{s\ge1}(1/s!)g_s((\sum_{i\ge1}f_i(w^i)/i!)^s)=g_*(f_*(w))$. The regrouping is finite modulo $F^N$, since each input has filtration at least one and all terms with input count at least $N$ vanish there. Equivalently $GF(e^w)=G(e^{f_*(w)})=e^{g_*(f_*(w))}$, and projection to $T$ gives the same result.

The identity Taylor family has only its linear term nonzero, so its Taylor pushforward is $w$ itself. Composition is associative because composition of the continuous coalgebra maps is associative; it can also be read from refinement of the finite set partitions modulo each filtration quotient. Together with the preceding calculations this proves all the claims on actual solution sets.
